newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's Congress names Alarcon new president.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's Congress names Alarcon new president.

text.p: Ecuador's Congress on Tuesday named its leader, Fabian Alarcon, as the country's new president for the second time in five days, capping a turbulent week in Ecuadorean politics.

The vote was passed by an overwhelming 57-2 majority in the 82-member Congress, with five abstentions and one blank vote, and signalled an end to a bizarre political crisis triggered by last week's ouster of populist leader Abdala Bucaram.
Alarcon was not present in Congress at the time of the vote, which ended more than four hours of sometimes colourful debate. He was expected to give a news conference later.

The week's political turmoil, which at one point saw three people claiming the presidency, began on Thursday with the dismissal by a divided Congress of Bucaram, a quirky populist whose antics earned him the nickname "El Loco" (The Madman). The 49-year-old Alarcon was swiftly sworn in as the new president.

Carnival-like confusion ensued, with the defiant Bucaram initially refusing to step down and doing so only when the military withdrew its support. In turn, Vice President Rosalia Arteaga claimed transitional power under what she said were constitutional rules.

Alarcon, the 41st president in Ecuador's 167-year history, is to hand over power on Aug. 10, 1998, to a new democratically elected head of state. General elections are tentatively scheduled for early next year.

Ecuador's shaky transition process, which many bemused observers saw as another surreal episode in Latin America's unpredictable politics, remained clouded to the end by Arteaga's insistence on following the Constitution and not stepping down.

Arteaga, who became Ecuador's first woman president on Sunday when she took over as head of a caretaker government, bowed to pressure and left the presidential palace on Tuesday night, returning to her private residence.

At a hastily arranged news conference shortly after the start of the congressional session, she called for a referendum within three months to solve what she called the country's "constitutional void."

Embittered by legislators' refusal to hear her at the extraordinary session -- the congressional palace's main door remained shut when she showed up -- she said the referendum would ask Ecuadoreans to approve the creation of a constitutional assembly for reforming the State.

Arteaga, a 40-year-old lawyer and former education minister who was Bucaram's vice president, said Congress was not constitutionally empowered to appoint presidents. Denouncing "petty" interests, she lambasted "macho, arrogant" politicians motivated by "selfishness," saying she could be no part of "the grand bazaar of Ecuador's political class."
Some analysts said the "irrational" episode, which unfolded over carnival holidays, might leave deep scars on the small Andean nation's political scene.

"Politicians have shown an amazing lack of maturity," said Santiago Nieto, of the consulting firm Informe Confidencial. "They allowed everybody to see how power-hungry they were and how little they cared about the country's interests."
Another analyst, who requested anonymity, said Bucaram's swift dismissal on grounds of "mental incompetence" could set a dangerous precedent.
"Sane leaders could be given the boot for the same crazy reasons ... if the Constitution is not reformed, it will happen again," he said.
The accord paving the way for Alarcon to become president specified he could be appointed by a simple majority of Congress, without any constitutional reforms.
Bucaram dismissed the vote as a sham and a "national disgrace" and said Ecuador had fallen into the hands of "a traitor, a Judas."
"Some countries won't see kindly that Ecuador has a president (who is the) product of a dictatorship," he said.
Bucaram arrived in Panama on Tuesday evening, the first stop on a tour to tell regional leaders that he was deposed in what he called a military-backed "congressional coup."

He told reporters he would denounce that "corruption has taken over in Ecuador." From Panama, he said he would go on to Argentina to meet President Carlos Menem, then to Colombia and maybe Haiti, before returning to Panama for talks with President Ernesto Perez Balladares, currently in London.

Bucaram said he would return to Ecuador next weekend. Rumours immediately circulated that he would stay abroad, possibly in Panama, where he fled to a few years ago when he was mayor of Guayaquil after he was charged with corruption.
